text: Hello, world. Welcome back to the Four Eyes Report. Today: how Koreans drink, what they snack on, and what's changing in Korea right now.

text: Let's talk about drinking. By some statistics, Korea once ranked near the top of the world in alcohol per person. Numbers differ by source, but Koreans drank a LOT.

text: I believe it! Korean restaurants never turn their lights off. Twenty-four hours!

text: But that's changing. In OECD data, Korea has dropped to twenty-first as of 2021, and soju output has fallen three years in a row.

text: Wait, soju is down?! Soju is SO hot overseas right now!

text: Koreans still drink. Just not like before. It went from a marathon to a brisk walk.

text: And the taste changed too. First everyone loved wine, and now whisky is the cool one, right?

text: Yes. "A bottle of soju for the lady at the next table!" is out. "A glass of whisky" has more style.

text: Smooth. Very smooth.

text: The biggest change is the honsul bar. Koreans used to drink in big groups. Now younger people enjoy a good drink alone.

text: But everyone there is single, and hot, so it turns into a place to meet people!

text: You sit alone, you use a nickname, and you talk only if you want to.

text: Okay, next time I'm in Korea, I'm going!

text: One warning. There's no age limit. But Korea has "ip-ppaen": getting turned away at the door. Officially, never. In a bar full of young people, you can feel it.

text: Feel what?

text: Every head turning to say, "Sir... are you lost?"

text: Don't worry, Master K. I'll vouch for you at the door.

text: Thank you. I'll just drink at home.

text: Did somebody say "home"? I brought snacks. Do you know bunsik? Korean snack food. And here's the thing: Koreans are shocked that it's popular overseas.

text: Because bunsik is classic street food. Spicy, salty, sweet, and you can find it almost anywhere in Korea.

text: Mostly students. After school, they pool their allowance and share one plate of tteokbokki.

text: Enough food. Let's talk about how young Koreans are feeling. Spoiler: bored.

text: Korea has a word for the moment a hobby suddenly stops being fun. "Taegi."

text: A word for that? Like, "I used to love running, now I hate my shoes"?

text: Exactly. Golf-taegi. Running-taegi. Reading-taegi. Add it to anything that stopped being fun.

text: A Seoul trend forecaster even named "the age of boredom" the first trend of 2027. Too much stimulation, so nothing feels interesting.
